notes: Kingship or reign: God's rule, not mainly a territory. Matthew usually says "kingdom of heaven" where Mark and Luke say "kingdom of God," likely a reverent Jewish way of referring to God without naming him. It's the theme of Jesus' preaching from his first words (4:17).

Fairness and rightness in dealings with others.
Being declared in the right before God (especially in Paul).

range.note: Make something full, like a net (13:48).
Finish or bring to an end.

Fulfilling what is written in the law.

Regret and leave behind what was wrong.
A new direction for the whole life.

Joy in heaven over one who repents.

notes: Originally a priestly class among the Medes and Persians. By the first century the word covered experts in stars, dreams, and hidden knowledge, and could also mean a sorcerer. Matthew doesn't say how many came or that they were kings; those ideas came later.

notes: Describes someone in a good place, especially as God sees it. It's a declaration, not an instruction: Jesus isn't telling people to mourn, but saying that those who mourn are in God's favor. Some translations try "happy," which can sound too light.

Blessed are those who haven't seen and believe.
Blessed is the one who endures trials.

elsewhere.note: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!"

Reading the sky but not the times.
On healing on the Sabbath.

notes: The right or power to act, often given by someone higher. Matthew comes back to it: Jesus teaches with authority (7:29), forgives sins with it (9:6), gives it to the twelve (10:1), and at the end says "all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me" (28:18).

range.note: Permission or freedom to do something.

God's faithful kindness to his people.

Justice, mercy, and faithfulness.

notes: An upright stake, and the cross used for crucifixion. Rome reserved this execution for slaves, rebels, and the lowest criminals, and the condemned carried the crossbeam to the place of death. Jesus uses the image for following him (10:38) before he goes to the cross himself (27:32).

range.note: The wooden frame used for crucifixion.
The execution itself.
A picture of giving up one's life.

elsewhere.note: "Take up their cross and follow me."
Simon of Cyrene carries the cross.
The message of the cross.
Obedient to death on a cross.

notes: The wooden crossbar that joined two animals so they could pull together, and so a picture of work, service, and someone else's direction. Jewish teachers spoke of "the yoke of the law" or "the yoke of the kingdom." Jesus offers his own yoke as easy, and himself as a gentle teacher. The word can also mean a pair of scales (Revelation 6:5).

range.note: The frame joining working animals.
Obligations someone places on you, like slavery or a law.
A balance for weighing.

elsewhere.note: A yoke neither we nor our ancestors could bear.
Don't submit again to a yoke of slavery.
Those under the yoke of slavery.
A rider holding a pair of scales.

notes: The Greek form of the Hebrew shabbat, the seventh day of rest from Friday evening to Saturday evening. Keeping it was one of the clearest marks of Jewish identity. The plural can also mean "the week."

range.note: The seventh day, set apart for rest.
As in "the first day of the week" (28:1).

elsewhere.note: "The Sabbath was made for people."
A synagogue leader objects to Sabbath healing.
A healing on the Sabbath at the pool.
After the Sabbath, the first day of the week.

range.note: Something that identifies, like a signal.
A wonder that points to God's work.
A sign of what is coming.

elsewhere.note: Again, only the sign of Jonah.
Water into wine, the first of his signs.
Jews ask for signs.
"This will be a sign for you."

notes: From a verb meaning "to set side by side": a comparison that lays one thing next to another. It translates the Hebrew mashal, which covers proverbs, riddles, and illustrative stories. Matthew uses it a great deal; chapter 13 gathers seven parables in a row.

range.note: One thing set beside another to explain it.
A short story with a point, like the sower.
A saying that needs thinking about.

elsewhere.note: He taught them many things in parables.

The lost sheep.
Isaac received back "in a figure."

notes: A secret that has to be revealed, not a puzzle to solve. In the New Testament it usually means something God has kept hidden and now makes known. In Matthew the mysteries of the kingdom are given to the disciples, though what makes them "insiders" is that they ask and listen.

range.note: Something hidden until it is disclosed.
God's plan, now made known.
In wider Greek, the secret rites of a cult.

elsewhere.note: The secret of the kingdom of God.
The mystery kept secret for long ages.
The mystery made known by revelation.
"Listen, I tell you a mystery."

notes: Literally "to bring together": to put the pieces into a whole. In chapter 13 it's the dividing line. People who hear the word without understanding it are the path and rocky soil; the one who hears and understands is the good soil. The quotation from Isaiah turns on the same word.

range.note: Take in what something means.
See how things fit together.

elsewhere.note: "Hear and understand."
They hadn't understood about the loaves.
He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.
Paul quotes the same Isaiah passage.

notes: A builder who worked with wood and often stone, so "carpenter" can be too narrow. Matthew has the villagers call Jesus "the carpenter's son"; Mark's Gospel has them call Jesus himself a tekton. Either way, it places him in a working family that the whole village knew.

range.note: A worker in wood.
A craftsman in wood, stone, or building generally.

elsewhere.note: "Isn't this the carpenter?"

notes: A word Matthew uses mostly for the disciples, built from "little" and "faith." It describes faith that is real but small, not an absence of faith: they follow Jesus and still panic in a storm (8:26), forget the bread (16:8), and sink on the water (14:31); in the sermon it's said to listeners who worry about clothes (6:30). Luke uses it once.

range.note: Real trust that gives way under pressure.

elsewhere.note: Worry about clothing.
The storm on the lake.
The disciples forget the bread.
Luke's version of the clothing saying.

notes: Literally "to kiss toward": to bow or kneel before someone as a sign of honor or homage. It covers everything from showing respect to a ruler to worshiping God, so the context decides. Matthew uses it for the magi (2:2), for people kneeling before Jesus with a request (8:2, 9:18, 15:25), and for the disciples' worship (14:33, 28:17).

range.note: Show honor to a superior.
Come humbly with a request.
Give God the honor due to him.

elsewhere.note: "Worship the Lord your God."
They worshiped him, though some doubted.
Worship in spirit and truth.
Cornelius bows to Peter, who lifts him up.

notes: Something handed down: teaching or practice passed from one generation to the next. It isn't bad in itself. Paul praises good traditions and tells churches to hold them. Jesus' complaint in chapter 15 is about a particular tradition used to set aside a commandment.

range.note: Teaching or custom passed down.
The Pharisees' accumulated rulings on living out the law.

elsewhere.note: "The tradition of the elders."
Paul, zealous for the traditions of his ancestors.
Paul praises them for holding to the traditions.
"Hold to the traditions you were taught."

notes: From koinos, "common": to make something common rather than set apart, and so ritually unclean. In Jewish usage, "common" was the opposite of "holy." Jesus moves the question from outside to inside: what makes a person unclean is what comes from the heart.

range.note: Treat as ordinary, not set apart.
Ritually defile.
Treat what is holy as common.

elsewhere.note: The parallel saying.
"Don't call common what God has cleansed."
Accused of defiling the temple.
Sprinkling for those who are defiled.

notes: A diminutive of the word for dog, used in Matthew and Mark only in the story of the Canaanite woman. Matthew uses the plain word for dog elsewhere (7:6), as an insult for people outside. Here the woman picks up the small word Jesus used and turns it into a plea.
uncertain: Whether the diminutive softens the saying, pointing to household pets rather than street dogs, is debated, as is how Jesus intends the whole exchange.

range.note: A small dog, a household pet in many homes.
Gentiles could be called dogs by some Jews.

elsewhere.note: Mark's version: "it is not good to take the children's bread."
"Even the little dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs."

notes: From "to call out": a gathering of people called together. In everyday Greek it was a city's citizen assembly. The Greek Old Testament used it for Israel's assembly before God, which is the background Jesus' first hearers would hear. Matthew uses it only twice, here and in 18:17, and none of the other three Gospels uses it at all.

range.note: A city's gathering of free citizens.
God's gathered people in the Greek Old Testament.
A particular congregation.
All followers of Jesus.

elsewhere.note: "Tell it to the church."
Israel as "the assembly in the wilderness."
An unruly civic assembly in Ephesus.
Christ loved the church.

notes: A mass of rock or bedrock, in contrast to a loose stone. Jesus plays on Peter's name: Petros (a masculine name form) and petra. Many readers have noted that in Aramaic the same word would stand for both. In Matthew it also means the rock a wise builder chooses (7:24) and the rock cut for Jesus' tomb (27:60).
uncertain: What "this rock" refers to (Peter himself, his confession, or Jesus) has been debated among Christian traditions for centuries.

range.note: Solid rock, a foundation.
A rock face or ledge.
In the Psalms, God as a rock and refuge.

elsewhere.note: The wise builder on the rock.
"The rock was Christ."
A rock that makes people fall.
A rock of offense.

notes: To change form, the root of English "metamorphosis." It's used only four times in the New Testament: Jesus' transfiguration (here and in Mark) and twice for believers being changed, in Romans 12:2 and 2 Corinthians 3:18.

range.note: As on the mountain.
As in Paul's letters.

elsewhere.note: The same event in Mark.
"Be transformed by the renewing of your mind."
Being transformed into the same image.

notes: Originally the trigger of a trap, the thing that springs it. In the New Testament it's a stumbling block, something that trips a person up in following God. Peter becomes one for Jesus when he tries to talk him out of the cross, and Paul later says the cross itself is a stumbling block to many.

range.note: The part of a trap that snaps shut.
Something that makes a person fall.
A cause of taking offense.

elsewhere.note: "Woe to the world because of stumbling blocks."
A stone that makes people stumble.
Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews.
The offense of the cross.

notes: A young child, small enough to be carried and watched over. It's a diminutive of pais, "child," and is the word Jesus uses when he places a child among the disciples. In that world a child had no standing or power, which is the point Jesus draws: greatness in the kingdom runs through humility and dependence.

range.note: A small child or infant.
The dependent, humble stance Jesus commends.

elsewhere.note: "Let the little children come to me."
The same scene in Mark.
The same scene in Luke.
"Don't be children in your thinking."

notes: The Greek form of the Hebrew Ge Hinnom, the Valley of Hinnom just south of Jerusalem. In the Old Testament it's where some of Judah's kings sacrificed children, and the prophets spoke of it as a place of judgment. By Jesus' time it had become a name for the place of final judgment. Matthew uses it more than any other Gospel.
uncertain: A popular claim says Gehenna was Jerusalem's burning garbage dump. Scholars debate this: the idea isn't found in sources before the Middle Ages, and the Old Testament links the valley with child sacrifice.

range.note: The Valley of Hinnom near Jerusalem.
A picture of final judgment by fire.

elsewhere.note: "In danger of the fire of Gehenna."
"Fear the one who can destroy both soul and body."
The parallel about the hand that causes stumbling.
The tongue is set on fire by Gehenna.

notes: Literally "to send away" or "to let go." The same verb is used for leaving something behind (the fishermen left their nets), for allowing something, and for releasing someone from a debt or a sin. That second sense is why the story of the servant, where a debt is let go, and the call to forgive fit together so closely. STEPBible tags these senses separately: "leave," "forgive," and "permit."

range.note: Leave something or someone behind.

Release someone from sin or offense.
Allow or let.

elsewhere.note: They left their nets.
"Your sins are forgiven."
"Forgive us our sins."

notes: Originally a weight, then the largest unit of money in the ancient world: roughly 6,000 denarii, or about 6,000 days' wages. Ten thousand (a "myriad," the biggest single number word in Greek) talents is deliberately beyond anything repayable. Matthew is the only New Testament writer who uses the word, here and in the parable of the talents (chapter 25). English "talent" for ability comes from that later parable, not from the word's original meaning.

range.note: A large measure of weight, roughly 60 to 75 pounds.
The largest unit of currency.

elsewhere.note: Five, two, and one talent in the parable.
The servant hid his talent in the ground.
"Take the talent from him."
